paragraphs.heading: What it studies
paragraphs.text: Thermodynamics is the branch of physics about heat, work and temperature, and how they connect to energy, entropy and the properties of matter and radiation. Four laws govern how these quantities behave. The laws describe things you can measure in bulk, but statistical mechanics can explain them through the tiny particles underneath. The subject is used across science and engineering, from physical chemistry and biochemistry to mechanical engineering and the study of weather.

paragraphs.heading: Systems and surroundings
paragraphs.text: The subject studies how huge collections of objects interact. Its central ideas are a system and its surroundings. A system is made of particles whose average motions set its properties, and equations of state tie those properties to each other. Combining them gives internal energy and thermodynamic potentials, which help predict balance and changes that happen on their own. With these tools, thermodynamics describes how systems respond to changes around them, in engines, phase transitions, chemical reactions and even black holes.

paragraphs.heading: The laws
paragraphs.text: The four laws are the starting rules for describing any such system. The first law says energy can pass between systems as heat, as work, or by moving matter. The second law brings in entropy, a quantity that shows which direction a system can change in. Entropy also measures how ordered a system is and how much useful work can be drawn out of it.

paragraphs.heading: Pumps and pressure
paragraphs.text: The history of the field usually starts with Otto von Guericke, who in 1650 built the world's first vacuum pump. He wanted to disprove Aristotle's old belief that nature abhors a vacuum. Robert Boyle heard of the design and in 1656, working with Robert Hooke, built an air pump of his own. With it they saw that pressure, temperature and volume are connected. In time this became Boyle's Law, which says pressure and volume are inversely proportional.

paragraphs.heading: From steam to science
paragraphs.text: Thermodynamics grew out of a wish to make early steam engines more efficient. In 1679 Denis Papin built a steam digester, a closed vessel that held in steam until the pressure rose high, and its moving valve gave him the idea of a piston and cylinder engine. Building on his designs, Thomas Savery made the first engine in 1697, and Thomas Newcomen followed in 1712. Joseph Black worked out heat capacity and latent heat, and James Watt's external condenser made steam engines much more efficient. In 1824 Sadi Carnot published Reflections on the Motive Power of Fire, which marked the start of thermodynamics as a modern science.

paragraphs.heading: The laws take shape
paragraphs.text: The first and second laws appeared together in the 1850s, mainly through the work of William Rankine, Rudolf Clausius and William Thomson, also known as Lord Kelvin. Rankine wrote the first textbook on the subject in 1859. Clausius stated the core ideas of the second law in 1850 and introduced entropy in 1865. Physicists including James Clerk Maxwell, Ludwig Boltzmann and Max Planck laid the foundations of statistical thermodynamics.

paragraphs.heading: Branches of the field
paragraphs.text: Soon after its start with engines, the subject spread to chemical compounds and reactions. Chemical thermodynamics looks at the role of entropy in reactions and has supplied most of the field's growth. Statistical thermodynamics predicts how large numbers of particles move together from their tiny-scale behavior, and in 1909 Constantin Carathéodory offered a purely mathematical version built on axioms. Classical thermodynamics mainly studies systems in equilibrium, while the study of systems out of equilibrium is often handled as an add-on to that classical form.
